title: How Gender Medicine Set Itself Up for Disaster
author: Benjamin Ryan
content:
![How Gender Medicine Set Itself Up for
Disaster](https://www.compactmag.com/content/images/2026/04/AP26051696702127.jpg)

At a closed-door meeting in 2021, ACLU attorney Chase Strangio declared, "If
we take away these health care options, kids are going to die." The scrappy
litigator uttered this dire proclamation in an address at the biennial
conference of [_USPATH_](https://wpath.org/uspath/?ref=compactmag.com), the US
branch of the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, or
[_WPATH_](https://wpath.org/?ref=compactmag.com). Strangio [_has
played_](https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/power/2025/06/16/chase-strangio-
transgender-rights-supreme-court/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) a [_pivotal
role_](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/19/magazine/scotus-transgender-care-
tennessee-skrmetti.html?ref=compactmag.com) in the transgender movement's
general refusal to offer concessions on the chief principles animating its
cause. Most central, and controversial, has been [_the
demand_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/heightened-scrutiny-scapegoats-
the?ref=compactmag.com) that minors identifying as transgender have access to
gender-transition treatments, including puberty blockers, [_cross-sex
hormones_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/1-in-1000-privately-
insured-17-year?ref=compactmag.com), and
[_surgeries_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/how-harvard-teed-up-the-false-
claim?ref=compactmag.com).

Speaking to USPATH, Strangio entreated attendees to infuse legal and political
advocacy into their work as doctors and mental-health providers. This battle
cry was tempered with a foreboding vision of a dystopian future, one with "so
many catastrophic outcomes" and a legal landscape for transgender people in
which it could become "impossible for us to survive." Bans on pediatric gender
medicine--which at the time of the meeting [_had
passed_](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/03/25/lgbtq-rights-gop-
bills-dont-say-gay/?ref=compactmag.com) in [_only one
state_](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2021/apr/06/arkansas-transgender-
youth-gender-affirming-treatment-ban?ref=compactmag.com)--were just "an entry
point," Strangio prophesied, to "banning care for all trans people."

The subsequent years would actually deliver a more drastic cascade of defeat
than Strangio envisioned. Today, bans of gender-transition interventions for
minors [_blanket_](https://www.lgbtmap.org/equality-
maps/healthcare/youth_medical_care_bans?ref=compactmag.com) more than half of
US states. And the second Trump administration has [_run
roughshod_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/hospitals-giving-gender-
treatments?ref=compactmag.com) over this beleaguered field, using the might of
[_multiple_](https://x.com/FBI/status/1929587710894739567?ref=compactmag.com)
[_federal_](https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-acts-bar-hospitals-performing-
sex-rejecting-procedures-children.html?ref=compactmag.com)
[_agencies_](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/department-justice-subpoenas-
doctors-and-clinics-involved-performing-transgender-
medical?ref=compactmag.com) to
[_bring_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/17/nyregion/nyu-hospital-
transgender-youth.html?ref=compactmag.com) [_it to
heel_](https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2025/07/31/ui-health-suspends-
gender-affirming-surgeries-for-patients-under-19?ref=compactmag.com). In the
face of this onslaught, WPATH has not budged. And having
[_asserted_](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/26895269.2022.2100644?__cf_chl_tk=pcPUrGddvmMdzf.xVw.vQcuA.T97zm_WLD5lqcktpbQ-1773695548-1.0.1.1-uioIRK0VHtrZAcNEViS0aE1r6sWEEqFgbac1G3CblPM&ref=compactmag.com)
itself as the [_decisive authority_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX189-560-39-WPATH-16-REDACTED.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
on caring for youth identifying as transgender, WPATH's leaders have made
their organization's own reputation inseparable from pediatric gender
medicine's. If one goes south, so goes the other.

Now we have a new, wide-open window into the workings of this influential and
secretive organization, thanks to a pivotal legal case in Alabama. In 2022,
families represented by ACLU attorneys and other litigators [_sued the
state_](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/families-sue-alabama-over-felony-
ban-gender-affirming-care-transgender-adolescents?ref=compactmag.com) over its
pediatric gender medicine ban. The state responded by subpoenaing WPATH's
internal records after a judge established WPATH's transgender-care guidelines
were the linchpin for validating these medical practices as safe and
effective. A portion of the resulting trove was [_unsealed in
2024_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/boe-v-marshall/?ref=compactmag.com). In June
2025, the remaining subpoenaed cache was unsealed. In the fall, all those
files landed on my computer. This is the story those records--almost all of
them previously unreported--told.

* * *

Unlike most scientific meetings, WPATH and USPATH conferences are a black box
to outsiders. The events are closed to journalists and attendees are forbidden
to photograph or record the presentations. Consequently, my access to almost
500 conference videos granted me an unprecedented, unobstructed survey of four
of these gatherings, spanning from 2021 to 2023.

> "WPATH and USPATH conferences are a black box to outsiders."

This catalogue, which WPATH fought to keep shielded, provides a rich account
of how leading figures in pediatric gender medicine approached scientific
research, drove the evolution of medical practices, and strategized
politically during a critical turning point in this field's brief and tortured
history. The two years following Strangio's 2021 address were a period in
which statehouse Republicans [_escalated_](https://www.thedissident.news/the-
ratchet/?ref=compactmag.com) their attacks on this field. The WPATH conference
presenters largely responded to the political siege by doubling down. Rather
than engage in soul searching over whether their methods in pediatrics were
ethically sound and whether any criticisms had merit, they overwhelmingly
stuck to their guns.

At the 2022 conference, Dr. Maddie Deutsch, then USPATH's president,
discouraged colleagues from referencing too many potential harms of treatment
in public-facing materials, for fear they will be leveraged against the field.
Deutsch, the medical director of the University of California San Francisco's
gender clinic, had the previous year led the charge to censure her former
colleague, psychologist Erica Anderson, for airing dirty laundry. Anderson,
who preceded Deutsch as USPATH president, had
[_told_](https://www.thefp.com/p/top-trans-doctors-blow-the-
whistle?ref=compactmag.com) journalist Abigail Shrier that some pediatric
providers were providing "sloppy" care. During a tense subsequent exchange
over talking to journalists, Anderson warned USPATH that stonewalling the
press would only worsen the crisis facing the organization. Deutsch took a
different course. She orchestrated a moratorium on USPATH leadership speaking
to the media.

The example USPATH made of Anderson, who left WPATH in dismay and became one
of the field's few vocal dissidents, could help explain the remarkably little
overt disagreement during the conference sessions. True, some may have
occurred in private side conversations. But such a paucity of robust internal
debate during sessions is, to say the least, uncommon at a medical conference.
And this particular society, which unlike most traditional medical
associations allows non-care-providers such as activists and lawyers to join,
is evidently structured to operate by its own rules. The organization,
Anderson told me, "shifted into high gear on advocacy as I decided to
withdraw. There was no reasoning with them."

WPATH would have the public believe that it merely follows the science. "We
promote free and full discussion of scientific ideas," WPATH asserts in its
[_code of conduct policy_](https://wpath.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/WPATH-
Code-of-Conduct-Policy-REVISED-Sep-10-2025.pdf?ref=compactmag.com). And in a
video from a 2023 WPATH conference devoted to training care providers, Jamison
Green, a legal and policy scholar and past president of the organization,
insisted: "WPATH doesn't function as an advocacy organization any more than
other medical professional associations do."

The videos present a different reality. Presenters frequently downplayed
fundamental hazards about irrevocably altering adolescents' bodies. Meanwhile,
a parade of systematic reviews--the gold standard of scientific evidence--was
concluding [_that the evidence_](https://archive.is/oTKaw?ref=compactmag.com)
[_backing_](https://palveluvalikoima.fi/documents/1237350/22895008/Valmistelumuistion%20Liite%201.%20Kirjallisuuskatsaus.pdf/5ad0f362-8735-35cd-3e53-3d17a010f2b6/Valmistelumuistion%20Liite%201.%20Kirjallisuuskatsaus.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
pediatric gender medicine is [_weak and
inconclusive_](https://adc.bmj.com/content/110/6/429?ref=compactmag.com).
These findings have led health authorities in a number of European nations,
concerned about risks such as infertility, to [_reverse
course_](https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2023/04/gender-affirming-
care-debate-europe-dutch-protocol/673890/?ref=compactmag.com). They
reclassified pediatric gender-transition interventions as experimental and
sharply restricted minors' access.

Not WPATH. The organization remained on an inexorable trajectory in the
opposite direction, toward its eventual head-on collision with the second
Trump administration.

In response to detailed questions, a WPATH spokesperson replied: "For nearly
50 years, WPATH has been committed to advancing evidence-informed care for
transgender people worldwide, setting a global standard for clinical
excellence that's grounded in established scientific standards,
multidisciplinary expertise, and peer-reviewed research. As with most
scientific bodies, we welcome open debate and the free exchange of ideas and
diverse viewpoints because it sharpens best practices and strengthens the
integrity of the scientific process. WPATH's dedication to ethical care and
the health and well-being of the patient community we serve remains
unwavering."

Except when specified, no one else referenced in this article from WPATH or
its conferences and responded to a detailed request for comment.

* * *

It's likely no one has done more to push pediatric gender medicine toward more
liberal prescribing practices than Dr. Johanna Olson-Kennedy, who [_until
recently_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/dr-johanna-olson-kennedys-
pediatric?ref=compactmag.com) directed the gender clinic at Children's
Hospital Los Angeles. Charismatic and indefatigable, the pediatrician has been
particularly vocal in questioning the comprehensive psychosocial assessments
WPATH's guidelines recommend for minors seeking gender-transition
interventions. What some have held up as invaluable safeguards, [_she has
disparaged_](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLdMrbgYfVl-uRbb-
KAAkSNzi_gHzQAX2d&ref=compactmag.com) as stigmatizing and counterproductive.

Over the past decade, Olson-Kennedy's vision for pediatric gender medicine has
increasingly [_won
out_](https://archive.is/20241031175221/https:/www.nysun.com/article/shocking-
and-reckless-top-gender-clinic-assesses-children-for-gender-altering-medical-
treatments-in-just-2-hours-lawsuit-lays-bare?ref=compactmag.com). It has
effectively edged out more cautious WPATH leaders, most notably psychologist
Laura Edwards-Leeper, who coauthored the chapters on children and adolescents
in WPATH's [_2022
guidelines_](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/26895269.2022.2100644?ref=compactmag.com).
Edwards-Leeper also co-wrote with Anderson a 2021 [__Washington Post_
editorial_](https://www.washingtonpost.com/outlook/2021/11/24/trans-kids-
therapy-psychologist/?ref=compactmag.com) in which they called out
recklessness in the field and championed a re-commitment to psychological
exploration with young patients.

Edwards-Leeper spent years playing the Cassandra foil to what she saw as
Olson-Kennedy's hubris. She told me she "repeatedly, like a broken record,
warned colleagues" that the field's unwieldy practices would inspire a
backlash that, above all, would hurt the children they all sought to help. But
WPATH leadership, Edwards-Leeper said, ignored her expressed concerns.

"I naively believed they would actually use their power to get the ship back
on course," she told me. They did not. So like Anderson, she finally gave up
and left the organization. WPATH had closed ranks.

In the conference videos, WPATH members rarely put into plain language any
concern that adolescents might ever be mistaken about being transgender.
Instead, they emphasized centering the "lived experience" of trans children.
Few granted much merit to parents' objections or concerns about consenting to
their child's desire for permanent, body-altering treatments and
[_surgeries_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/at-least-14000-us-minors-have-
received?ref=compactmag.com).

Dr. Natasha Johnson, a pediatrician at McMaster University in Ontario,
reported at the 2022 conference that her team found no regret among 174
Canadian youth after two years of care at youth gender clinics. Any parent's
objection to gender-transition treatment, the researchers concluded, was not
tied to their children's own perspectives; and parental attitudes generally
improved over time. "This suggests that parents' feelings should not be
prioritized over the youth's experience," Johnson flatly said.

Ren Massey, a Georgia psychologist and coauthor of the WPATH guidelines'
adolescent chapter, in 2022 suggested bringing wary parents in line by
introducing the specter of a CPS call. "There are at least some child
protective service workers who are willing to enforce the need for affirmation
by parents, at least with social transition needs, names, pronouns, etc.,"
Massey said. "Even letting parents know that if that's true where you are
practicing, that might get their attention a little bit."

Such dismissive attitudes toward concerned parents prevailed among many in the
WPATH orbit even when, as was often the case, parents said their teenager's
gender-related distress seemed to have come from out of the blue. Similar
insouciance also tended to hold when the adolescent was saddled with multiple
[_comorbid_](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13034-015-0042-y?ref=compactmag.com)
[_psychiatric_](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165178122004875?ref=compactmag.com)
[_conditions_](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00049530.2021.1900747?ref=compactmag.com)
and
[_autism_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10313553/?ref=compactmag.com).

The videos further reveal a general lack of interest in why pediatric gender
dysphoria diagnoses had recently exploded and shifted from a small population
of mainly younger natal males presenting to youth gender clinics to a
[_throng_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/gender-dysphoria-surges-50-fold-
in?ref=compactmag.com) of mostly adolescent natal girls. Multiple presenters
heaped scorn on a controversial [_2018
paper_](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0202330&ref=compactmag.com)
in which physician and scientist Dr. Lisa Littman popularized the term "rapid-
onset gender dysphoria," or
[_ROGD_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/controversial-gender-
researchers?ref=compactmag.com), and cited social contagion as a potential
contributor.

Olson-Kennedy's opposition notwithstanding, WPATH's
[_guidelines_](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/26895269.2022.2100644?ref=compactmag.com)
do recommend a "comprehensive biopsychosocial assessment" for adolescents
seeking gender-transition interventions. And the guidelines highlight the
importance of parents' input and concerns. But the conference videos suggest a
gulf between WPATH's guidance and actual practice by at least some in its
membership. Dr. Scott Leibowitz, a child psychiatrist, current WPATH board
member, and coauthor of the 2022 guidelines' adolescent chapter, said at the
2023 training conference that the guidelines are "very flexible" and
essentially aspirational.

"What we're putting forward is more of a gold standard--not necessarily: '_You
must do this_ ,'" Leibowitz said.

Even presenters who favored a more cautious and circumspect approach often
characterized assessments primarily as a conduit for individualizing care.
They rarely made clear that the assessments were at least partly meant to
prevent poor outcomes by selecting out those who didn't meet diagnostic
criteria.

Florence Ashley, a law professor at the University of Alberta, is one of
academia's most aggressive
[_opponents_](https://www.florenceashley.com/uploads/1/2/4/4/124439164/ashley_adolescent_medical_transition_is_ethical.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
[_of
assessments_](https://www.florenceashley.com/uploads/1/2/4/4/124439164/ashley_et_al_do_gender_assessments_prevent_regret_in_transgender_healthcare_-
_a_narrative_review.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) or other "guardrails" for patients
of all ages seeking gender-transition interventions. At the 2022 conference,
Ashley insisted that doctors have historically required referral letters to
clear such patients "to essentially cover their ass."

> "Presenters often refashioned assessment to affirm identity."

Presenters often refashioned assessment to affirm identity and reduce barriers
to treatment and surgery. This dovetailed with an intense focus on how to
preserve access, expand capacity, and circumvent any obstacles, whether from
parents, insurers, legislators or care providers' reluctance or inadequate
training. This paradigm shift further merged with the
[_repurposing_](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hast.1583?ref=compactmag.com)
of the gender-affirming care model away from addressing psychopathology and
toward serving the patient's so-called "[_embodiment
goals_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35815503/?ref=compactmag.com)."

This term, which intertwines metaphysics with plastic surgery, was uttered ten
times in a session at the 2023 conference that offered a master class in the
Olson-Kennedy school of thought. A team of self-described "providers, clients,
advocates and activists" presented an assessment model they had spent two
years developing. As Amelia Brewer, an Oklahoma counselor, advised against
"lengthy or unnecessary protocols," the corresponding slide asserted that "one
session may be sufficient." All the slides warned: "DO NOT COPY OR RECORD."

Brewer further recommended providing a referral to a doctor who could
prescribe puberty blockers even before the end of the assessment process--if
delaying, she said, "would be a barrier to pausing irreversible changes."

Dianne Berg, a child psychologist at the University of Minnesota and coauthor
of the child chapter of WPATH's guidelines, was a rare voice expressing
concern about insufficient informed consent in her field. "It's been fairly
frequent," she said in 2022, that youth arrived at her practice already taking
blockers. This despite the fact that the parents and child often lacked even a
basic understanding of the drug's impacts, risks, and benefits. "It becomes
pretty clear that those important discussions either didn't happen or they
didn't happen in a way that they really stuck," Berg said. "That really
concerns me."

* * *

The potential for treatment or surgical regret, and the [_largely unknown
rate_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/how-common-is-
detransitioning?ref=compactmag.com) at which those who undergo gender-
transition interventions as minors might experience it, is one of the larger
elephants in the pediatric gender medicine exam room. Olson-Kennedy, who is
[_currently serving_](https://wpath.org/about/ec-bod/?ref=compactmag.com) as
USPATH's president, is notorious among critics of gender medicine for a [_one-
minute clip_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5Y6espcXPJk&ref=compactmag.com)
from an undercover video, shot and
[_published_](https://archive.org/details/olson-kennedy-breasts-go-and-get-
them) in 2018, in which she is captured [_responding
glibly_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/pediatric-gender-medicine-
doctor?ref=compactmag.com) to the suggestion that minors might regret gender-
transition mastectomies. "If you want breasts at a later point in your life,"
she quipped, "you can go and get them."

> "'If you want breasts at a later point in your life,' she quipped, 'you can
> go and get them."

In a video from the 2022 conference, Olson-Kennedy referenced the undercover
tape, grousing that after googling her name, "the first thing that you would
see is that I send healthy thirteen-year-old girls to have their breasts
removed, right? Because it came from a talk that somebody surreptitiously
recorded me talking. It was obviously way out of context." She suggested she
hadn't said anything objectionable. And yet, in Olson-Kennedy's 2018
[_paper_](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2674039?ref=compactmag.com)
documenting 68 youths' mastectomies, two were physically healthy thirteen-year
olds. And in the full fifty-three-minute [_undercover
video_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e9LbMIKdixo&ref=compactmag.com), she
expressed certainty that minors were mature enough to make many "life-altering
decisions" and suggested that any risk of the trans identity merely being a
phase should essentially be discounted.

In a 2023 conference session, Olson-Kennedy doubled down, saying: "I think
that a lot of this conversation outside of maybe these spaces gets talked
about through a lens of, like, 'How can we make sure people are really trans,'
right? And 'They're not going to regret their decision later?'" But, she
added, "that's actually not the discussion that I'm interested in
participating in. I'm interested in discussing and having a conversation about
giving the very best possible care to trans young people--the care that they
need and deserve." Many other presenters similarly disparaged using
assessments to scrutinize the veracity of a child's gender identity.

In 2024, Olson-Kennedy was [_sued for
malpractice_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/detransitioner-sues-johanna-
olson?ref=compactmag.com) by a former patient after signing off on the girl's
mastectomy when she was fourteen. It turned out the young woman did want
breasts later in life.

* * *

The WPATH conference videos shed light on a [_long-running
study_](https://reporter.nih.gov/search/OPTb_4f5-kOe2wU2YYzolA/project-
details/10615754?ref=compactmag.com) of pediatric gender-transition treatment
backed by some $10 million in federal grants. A decade ago, the study [_began
enrolling_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32839079/?ref=compactmag.com)
hundreds of youths with gender dysphoria, who were prescribed puberty blockers
or cross-sex hormones. The study has [_attracted
criticism_](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/06/15/magazine/gender-
therapy.html?ref=compactmag.com) for the languid pace at which its
investigators--Olson-Kennedy heads the team--have published about patient
outcomes.

At the 2021 conference, Olson-Kennedy reported data on the twelve-month mark
after over 300 youths were prescribed cross-sex hormones at ages twelve to
twenty. Mental health metrics improved modestly overall, primarily driven by
shifts in the biological girls, Olson-Kennedy disclosed. She suggested the
biological boys would improve in time, since the effects of estrogen take
longer to materialize. But the team's ultimate 2023
[_paper_](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1e-0vOrw6tK5SMWWi4fio_PKH9vbhiXFx/view?ref=compactmag.com)
on these youths' mental-health outcomes two years into the study still
documented [_only mild_](https://jessesingal.substack.com/p/the-new-highly-
touted-study-on-hormones?ref=compactmag.com) mental-health improvements and
only in biological girls.**** Two participants died by suicide--after starting
the hormones many in the field tout as "life-saving."

In October 2024, _The New York Times_
[_reported_](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/23/science/puberty-blockers-
olson-kennedy.html?ref=compactmag.com) that Olson-Kennedy had said she was
withholding publishing the long-awaited results of a puberty-blocker study,
and doing so for political reasons. Facing blowback, Olson-Kennedy
[_asserted_](https://x.com/LeorSapir/status/1860083848807387470?ref=compactmag.com)
the _Times_ had presented "an inaccurate and misrepresentative picture of the
status" of the study. _Times_ spokesperson Danielle Rhoades-Ha told me via
email: "We're confident in the accuracy of our reporting. The [
_story_](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/23/science/puberty-blockers-olson-
kennedy.html?ref=compactmag.com) was based on National Institute of Health
documents obtained via public records requests, as well as a lengthy, on-the-
record interview with Dr. Olson-Kennedy."

Olson-Kennedy's team [_finally released_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/long-
awaited-puberty-blockers-study?ref=compactmag.com) the paper in question in a
[_pre-print last
May_](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.05.14.25327614v1.full.pdf?ref=compactmag.com).
Unlike a foundational Dutch study
[_published_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20646177/?ref=compactmag.com) in
2011, it documented no mental-health shifts. Olson-Kennedy's team rationalized
that the young people were largely mentally well to begin with and simply
coasted on blockers. Journalist Jesse Singal
[_remarked_](https://jessesingal.substack.com/p/a-critique-of-mental-and-
emotional?ref=compactmag.com) that this assertion flew in the face of
[_claims_](https://www.nejm.org/doi/suppl/10.1056/NEJMoa2206297/suppl_file/nejmoa2206297_protocol.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
by [_Olson-Kennedy_](https://www.aclu.org/wp-
content/uploads/2023/07/059-Expert-Report-of-Johanna-Olson-Kennedy-MD-
MS.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) herself that youths with gender dysphoria were
often in emotional dire straits and in need of psychic relief from puberty
blockers.

The conference videos provide new insights into Olson-Kennedy's reasons for
delaying publication of her research and suggest how her thinking on the
matter changed over time. In 2021, Olson-Kennedy reported that her team had
amassed a trove of data from the federally backed study. Facing rising
political scrutiny, she suggested sunlight was the best disinfectant. "We want
to prioritize publishing this information because it needs to get out into the
general public while there is this ongoing attack on transgender youth and
transgender youth care," she said. By the 2023 conference, she reported her
team had up to seven years of follow-up data and were working on "several more
manuscripts." But now they were wary about publishing.

> "Now they were wary about publishing."

"I asked our person at the NIH if there was a prize for the grant that got the
most FOIA requests, and she said, 'No, but even if there was, you would still
be behind Covid and fluoride,'" Olson-Kennedy said, to laughter. Describing
her team's painstaking efforts to avoid providing fodder for a backlash,
Olson-Kennedy said, "Every single manuscript is absolutely impeccable with
what it is, what it is stating, the results that are being reported. We're
thinking about how things can be taken out of context and misused and
potentially come back and damage us."

At the prior year's conference, Olson-Kennedy's team reported that among the
nearly one in five youths in the study who were sexually active before
starting hormones, sexual satisfaction "did not improve after twenty-four
months." These findings remain unpublished.

* * *

The question of whether WPATH's north star was science or advocacy was central
to the legal dispute in Alabama that led the federal judge to unseal the
conference videos. The first cache of records Alabama subpoenaed, [_unsealed
in mid-2024_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/boe-v-marshall/?ref=compactmag.com),
buttressed the attorney general's case that WPATH is an activist organization
and therefore an unreliable arbiter of acceptable medical practices. Internal
emails documented WPATH leadership both
[_acknowledging_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX174-560-24-WPATH-1-REDACTED.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
that the science behind medically transitioning adolescents was weak and
noting that this fact could prove politically inconvenient. But these leaders
[_nevertheless
wrote_](https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/23/23-477/328275/20241015131826340_2024.10.15%20-%20Ala.%20Amicus%20Br.%20iso%20TN%20FINAL.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
in the adolescent chapter of the 2022 guidelines that such interventions were
"medically necessary."

In [_one email_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX4-557-4-Cantor-Supp.-Report-
App.-A-Sub.-UNSEALED.pdf?ref=compactmag.com), a guidelines author made
apparent reference to conferring with Chase Strangio, the ACLU litigator, on
drafting the document, stating, "Here are a number of my thoughts which may be
helpful for Chase and the legal team." At the 2021 conference, Strangio spoke
to his cross-pollination, saying, "I have collaborated with USPATH and WPATH
for the last decade in the work that I do." In another internal
[_document_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX174-560-24-WPATH-1-REDACTED.pdf?ref=compactmag.com),
a guidelines coauthor stated: "Our concerns, echoed by the social justice
lawyers we spoke with, is that evidence-based review reveals little or no
evidence and puts us in an untenable position in terms of affecting policy or
winning lawsuits."

An ACLU spokesperson responded to detailed questions with a statement: "The
ACLU remains committed to the principle that any decision about gender-
affirming medical treatments should be between transgender youth, their
families, and their doctors--not politicians. We will not apologize for our
advocacy or litigation on behalf of these families or their medical providers
in pursuit of their Constitutional rights and equal justice under law."

The subpoenaed WPATH emails [_also documented_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX4-557-4-Cantor-Supp.-Report-
App.-A-Sub.-UNSEALED.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) how a Biden administration health
official, Admiral Rachel Levine, [_pushed the
organization_](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/25/health/transgender-minors-
surgeries.html?ref=compactmag.com) to remove the age limits, citing political
motivation. WPATH resisted, but ultimately caved after the American Academy of
Pediatrics threatened to oppose the new guidelines if they retained the age
limits. Notably, the WPATH leaders struck the age limits without putting the
edit through their standard process for reaching internal consensus, known as
the Delphi method.

Eli Coleman, an emeritus professor of family medicine at the University of
Minnesota and co-chair of the WPATH guidelines-revision committee, later
emphasized in [_an email_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX188-700-17-WPATH-15-REDACTED-560-38.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
that WPATH's capitulation to the AAP was "highly confidential."

On September 21, 2022, a WPATH leader whose name is redacted
[_emailed_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX188-700-17-WPATH-15-REDACTED-560-38.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
colleagues to address the question of how to respond to reporters asking about
the age-limit removal, saying, "I think it's best we all get on the same exact
page, and PRONTO." Dr. Marci Bowers, a California gender-affirming surgeon and
WPATH's then-president-elect, replied that she'd told Reuters that the
organization had removed the age boundaries to prioritize "individualized
patient care." She said that "clamming up to the media is not a healthy
response and invites suspicion." In response to Bowers' narrative reframing, a
Dutch colleague replied, "I like this."

The [_unsealed emails_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX168-560-18-JHU-3.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) further
demonstrated that in service of crafting evidence-based guidelines, WPATH had
[_commissioned_](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/12/opinion/gender-affirming-
care-cass-review.html?ref=compactmag.com) from researchers at Johns Hopkins
University a series of systematic reviews of the research backing gender-
transition treatment. Then, evidently displeased with the reviews' findings,
WPATH leadership exerted heavy-handed control over what was meant to be an
independent process. Despite the fact that a Hopkins researcher [_indicated in
2019_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX167-560-17-JHU-2.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) they
were in the "process of completing systematic reviews addressing 34 questions
and 23 subquestions (plus those received in December)," only [_two
papers_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34993517/?ref=compactmag.com) were
ever
[_published_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894249/?ref=compactmag.com).

Last June, the Supreme Court effectively blessed bans on gender transition
treatments for minors. This was a crushing, if expected, [_blow to
Strangio_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/insidious-the-aclus-chase-
strangio?ref=compactmag.com), who argued the case for the ACLU. Under pressure
by Justice Samuel Alito during those [_oral
arguments_](https://www.supremecourt.gov/oral_arguments/argument_transcripts/2024/23-477_hgdj.pdf?ref=compactmag.com),
Strangio confessed there was "no evidence" to support the claim that these
interventions prevent suicide death, acknowledging this is "thankfully and
admittedly" rare among transgender youth. These admissions undermined the
central thesis of Strangio's 2021 USPATH speech: that state bans definitively
threatened the lives of youth seeking these interventions.

> "The conference videos offer further evidence of WPATH's shifting
> narrative."

The conference videos offer further evidence of WPATH's shifting narrative
about the age limits for gender treatments and surgeries. At the 2021
conference, Dr. Joshua Safer, an endocrinologist at Mount Sinai in New York
and a co-author of the upcoming hormones chapter revision, acknowledged the
"tension" in the pediatric gender medicine field about the age limits. Safer
said: "There are no plans with any of the guideline groups to do more than
recognize that tension, to say out loud that the age-based criteria are just
very, very rough guidance." When the
[_guidelines_](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/26895269.2022.2100644?ref=compactmag.com)
were published online on September 15, 2022, the age limits remained. But
WPATH took the document down that same day. When it was republished hours
later, the age limits had vanished.

Four days later, Leibowitz, who then ran the gender clinic at Nationwide
Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio, presented the new adolescent chapter to
the WPATH conference. Acknowledging the "risks associated" with "including or
not including age minimums," he enumerated various criteria he said should
take precedence, such as a child's maturity and ability to provide informed
consent. He added that "currently the final document landed on protecting the
criteria," because "ages were serving as a distracter from those important
criteria, and that would not have allowed for adolescents to access the care
that they need."

Referring to the use of the Delphi process to reach internal consensus in the
chapter's development, Leibowitz said, "Every single statement that you had
was voted on and went through that process." Leibowitz said this after having,
in [_an email_](https://www.alabamaag.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/SJ.DX186-700-15-WPATH-13-REDACTED-560-36.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
to coauthors of the pediatrics chapters the previous month, recapitulated the
group's concerns about potentially skirting the Delphi process if they removed
the age limits under political pressure from Levine (who [_later
denied_](https://benryan.substack.com/p/dr-rachel-levine-denies-having-
pressured?ref=compactmag.com) the pressure campaign). At the conference,
Leibowitz said that an age limit "also adds an arbitrary element to the
guidelines," and assured the audience that the age-limit issue "was thought
through a lot, and there was a lot of discussion about it."

That discussion had included a September 9, 2022, email Dr. Jon Arcelus,
cochair of the guidelines committee and a transgender medicine specialist at
the University of Nottingham, sent to Leibowitz, Coleman, and other WPATH
leaders. In it, Arcelus spelled out the AAP's demands, including "to remove
ages" from the guidelines.

Leibowitz did not mention to conference-goers the Biden administration's
contribution to any discussion about age limits or the AAP's successful effort
to get them removed from the guidelines.

In an October 3, 2022, email to a redacted recipient, Leibowitz reported his
efforts to keep WPATH leaders' story straight about the vanishing age limits.
"I'm hoping Marci [Bowers] takes my cue that we need to be coordinated with
the messaging," Leibowitz said. "I'm extremely worried." He then forwarded a
thread that included drafts of responses Bowers was preparing for a journalist
who sought answers about the age limits. Leibowitz said that his feedback to
Bowers's draft responses was highlighted in yellow. These were preceded by
Leibowitz's admonishment that Bowers should balance "what you feel to be true
with what we need to say."

One of the highlighted passages states, "I don't think we should specifically
name the AAP or necessarily emphasize/point to outside organization influence
(unless asked specifically)." In another draft response to the journalist,
Bowers wrote, "An individualized approach is the implication here." The
highlighted feedback reads: "I like this."

* * *

Of all the [_potential negative
impacts_](https://opa.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/2025-11/gender-dysphoria-
report.pdf?ref=compactmag.com) of providing minors puberty blockers and cross-
sex hormones,
[_infertility_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29963344/?ref=compactmag.com)
arguably poses the greatest [_ethical
quandary_](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1037/cpp0000230?ref=compactmag.com).
Multiple WPATH conference presenters reported that their young patients were
often naive about their future fertility needs. This included a panel from
Oregon Health & Science University, in which urologist Dr. Geolani Dy said
that for "a lot" of the hospital's young patients, the timing of a
vaginoplasty (a surgery that includes castration) "will fall around the
seventeen-, eighteen-year-old age range." Dutch researchers reported in
another session that among adults who medically transitioned in adolescence,
one fifth said they had been too young to make fertility decisions as minors.

"How many people have heard the adolescent say, 'I don't want to talk about
that. I'll just adopt'?" Leibowitz said in 2023 of his patients' blase
attitudes toward fertility preservation. "We've all heard them say that over
and over." But very few conference presenters suggested they observed any
ethical red line that would trigger a refusal to provide a minor a potentially
sterilizing intervention. Instead, their roadmap out of this ethical thicket
was invariably guided by more fertility counseling, more education, and more
informed consent.

> "Some bristled at the suggestion of hard age limits."

Some bristled at the suggestion of hard age boundaries. This included Sean
Moundas, a psychologist who in 2022 took umbrage at the fact that age limits
had been in the all-but-final draft of the revised WPATH guidelines. Such age
limits represent "adultism bias," he said.

"Any form of ageism is unethical," Simona Giordano, a bioethicist at the
University of Manchester and a member of WPATH's [_ethics
committee_](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/jpc.16734?ref=compactmag.com),
said the same year. "Refusing to treat someone because they are too young is
as unjust as refusing to treat someone because they are too old. Decisions
shouldn't be based on age, but on capacity to benefit from treatment."

Leibowitz spoke more frankly in 2023 about minors' varying degrees of
maturity. "Can every adolescent appreciate the lifelong implications of their
decisions? I'm sensing the parents probably are laughing," he said to
conference-goers. "I would say some can and some can't. Does that matter? I
guess so, when we're talking about long-standing decisions." He added that a
principal question to ask was: "How emotionally mature is the young person for
their age in terms of their decision-making capacity?" Leibowitz avoided
saying that a child should ever be refused treatment, but he did suggest
drawing out the assessment process for some youth before making the leap to
hormones. Otherwise, he infused the debate over the pediatric gender
medicine's weak evidence base with a civil-rights spirit. "Respecting human
rights is just as important as the evidence base," he said in 2022. "We work
within evidence-based medicine and evidence-based practice. But it's not the
only thing that can dictate what decisions get made."

* * *

In a mirror image of Olson-Kennedy's heel turn about publishing her data,
Maddie Deutsch by 2023 flipped about speaking to the media. But by then WPATH
was no longer merely defending the science. It had advanced to an active
training mode, politically and rhetorically, and was coaching members to
observe its rigidly prescribed terms. "The work that we do is important. It's
life-saving," Deutsch said at the 2023 conference. "And because this charge
does bring great responsibility, we have to be evidence-based. We have to be
measured--measured in our approach, measured in dealing with the press,
measured in dealing with conflict."

Deutsch announced that WPATH had brought in experts from the prominent
communications firm
[_BerlinRosen_](https://berlinrosen.com/?ref=compactmag.com) to advise
attendees on messaging. Other panels at that conference would counsel
attendees on interweaving the transgender and abortion rights fights and would
provide a crash course on "practical resistance" to "criminalization of
gender-expansive communities."

In a BerlinRosen training session devoted to "dispelling misinformation
through the media," PR mavens Laura Brandon and Kara Watkins-Chow advised
conference-goers on how to "disengage" from disfavored reporters. When giving
interviews, they advised, it was best to avoid delving into the finer details
of gender-transition treatment, which "could confuse or distract." Watkins-
Chow asserted that behind pediatric gender medicine "there is a body of
evidence that is strong" and that "blanket restrictions or limitations on care
based on age are really arbitrary." Brandon dismissed politicians' claims that
the field amounts to an "anomaly that's completely different from all other
health care."

A spokesperson from the firm said in a statement: "BerlinRosen proudly
partners with our clients to advance their goals, including on some of the
most complex, contested and significant issues of our time. We believe
strongly in the power of communications to elevate science-backed data and
research along with real-world human impacts to inform policy and improve
people's lives."

If Strangio spoke in 2021 as if on the brink of an ideological war, two years
later, Kellan Baker spoke as if commanding the troops in the thick of one.
Baker, then the executive director at the [_Whitman-Walker Institute for
Health Research & Policy_](https://www.whitman-
walker.org/institute/?ref=compactmag.com) in Washington, warned at the 2023
conference of "the creeping trend of fascism." The trans movement's
adversaries, he declared, were motivated in part by "a continuation of the
project of white supremacy." (This was after presenters across these
conferences repeatedly called apologetic attention to their own whiteness and
to the fact that WPATH's membership is overwhelmingly white, as are the
pediatric patients they care for, and as are the study participants they've
recruited.)

"I love a good trans agenda. I literally have whole text threads that are just
titled, like, _The Trans Agenda_ : 'This is what we're going to do!'" Baker
quipped. Citing US House Speaker Mike Johnson's references to "radical gender
ideology," he said, "Which is certainly what I subscribe to. I do, right--
don't we all?" Baker cited Dr. Miriam Grossman, a psychiatrist and ardent
opponent of pediatric gender medicine, who [_testified to
Congress_](https://www.congress.gov/118/meeting/house/116121/documents/HMTG-118-IF14-20230614-SD003.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
of certain "ignored" medical experts. He quoted her saying: "'They're against
medical interventions for the same reason these European countries are:
There's no evidence of long-term benefit.'" To which Baker replied: "I'm going
to go ahead and call bullshit on this whole thing." (He had truncated
Grossman's statement, which concluded: "...but there is evidence of harm.")

Such a sweeping dismissal is curious, given that Baker was the lead author of
one of the two systematic reviews WPATH commissioned that were ever published.
His [_2021
paper_](https://academic.oup.com/jes/article/5/4/bvab011/6126016?__cf_chl_tk=_lifrxAM2rgL5ah.atAz88SJJReTVcbsZ6.JIBTDgKA-1773763242-1.0.1.1-CZarvTnYEnl83ulG4EBecsApaNV4mWlP5ij6xfEQ6SQ&ref=compactmag.com)
examined studies on
[_two_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32368216/?ref=compactmag.com)
[_cohorts_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32144041/?ref=compactmag.com) who
were each followed for just 12 months and
[_another_](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25201798/?ref=compactmag.com)
followed for six years. His team found that hormone treatment was associated
with improved mental health metrics. However, they qualified this by writing:
"Certainty in this conclusion is limited by high risk of bias in study
designs, small sample sizes, and confounding with other interventions."

Baker and his colleagues also wrote that they "could not draw any conclusions
about death by suicide." In his conference speech, he hewed to that point.
Critics accurately asserted, he said, that "actually we don't have a lot of
good data about death by suicide." Undermining the central argument advocates
make to tout the benefits of gender-transition interventions for minors, he
advised against asserting they save lives. Baker further advised "avoiding
details like assigning ages to when people can get different types of care,"
because, he said, "care is individualized and age appropriate." It was best,
he said, to avoid the word "transition," which he said evoked the notion of
surgery, which he suggested the mainstream public might find objectionable.

Baker also counseled against using the term "gender-affirming care." Messaging
research indicated that when people hear that term, he said, "they think
'trans kids in the driver's seat.'" But he asserted this was an accurate
assessment. "Many of us here, I think we all support trans kids in the
driver's seat because it's their bodies, it's their lives," he said. "But when
you think about folks who don't know trans people, they are very scared by the
idea that young people are making irreversible decisions and that no one else
has any oversight over those decisions." With that in mind, he advised that
people instead use the term "medically necessary care."

* * *

What's most striking about the WPATH and USPATH conferences is what is not
discussed, and who is not there. Gone are Edwards-Leeper and Anderson. There
is no sign of Littman. I found no panels vigorously debating the ROGD
hypothesis. I witnessed no substantial discussions about whether to narrow
treatment criteria to weed out those for whom such radical alteration to their
bodies would be a [_catastrophic error_](https://www.thefp.com/p/a-legal-
first-that-could-change-gender?ref=compactmag.com).

For care providers inside the gender medicine echo chamber, it must really
come as a shock when outsiders voice objections to their methods. Because at
the conferences I observed, these professionals didn't expose their theories
to conflicting points of view. Even as a thought experiment, they almost never
entertained their opponents' arguments.

"The responsible action," Edwards-Leeper told me of WPATH, "would have been to
invite open dialogue, encourage critical thinking, take responsibility for
mistakes made, become more transparent with its members, patients and
families, and the media, and commit to moving the field forward based on
science rather than politics and activism. It is upsetting that they chose to
do none of that, but instead helped dig their own grave."

A culture that forbids internal debate will invariably fall into groupthink.
The textbook example of this tendency is the [_Challenger
explosion_](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1990-01207-001?ref=compactmag.com).
Leading up to the fateful 1986 launch, NASA leadership overrode internal
alarms that a constellation of factors were setting the stage for potential
catastrophe. The WPATH conference videos reveal a group of people enclosed in
a bubble, one they filled with so much hot air that it sent them soaring close
to the sun.

Is it any wonder that the whole enterprise is now crashing to the ground?
